options.why: It is a React DOM 19 feature that works without a framework.

explanation: React 19 manages stylesheets that have a `precedence` prop: it inserts each `href` once, orders sheets by precedence in `<head>`, and suspends rendering until they have loaded, so content never flashes unstyled. Without `precedence`, a `<link>` is treated like any other element.

)` produce `

`?

options.text: It separates two text nodes so hydration can match them
options.why: The browser would merge adjacent text into one node; the marker lets React split it back.

options.text: It is a debug marker that only appears in development builds of React
options.why: It is emitted in production too, because hydration needs it.

options.text: React encodes the space before `{name}` as an HTML comment for safety
options.why: The space stays as text. The comment sits between the two text parts.

options.text: It marks a Suspense boundary around the dynamic `{name}` value
options.why: Suspense boundaries use `<!--$-->` markers. This is a plain text separator.

explanation: The JSX has two text children, "Hello " and "Ada". Parsed HTML would merge them into one text node, leaving nothing to match each child to during hydration. React inserts an empty comment between adjacent text nodes. `renderToStaticMarkup`, which is not meant for hydration, omits it.

explanation: In development, React calls `Object.freeze` on each element's props object. In strict-mode code, assigning `props.title` throws a TypeError. {createPortal( , document.body )}

explanation: React runs capture handlers from the root down to the target, then bubble handlers from the target back up, all along the React tree. The portal does not change that, even though the button lives under `document.body` in the DOM.

stem:
In React 17 or later, what is logged when the button is clicked?

```jsx
document.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('document'));

<button onClick={(e) => { e.stopPropagation(); console.log('react'); }}>x</button>
```

options.why: React 17+ listens on the root container, so stopping propagation there keeps the event from `document`.
That was React 16, which listened on `document` itself, so it was already too late to stop.
The document listener is above the root, so it can only run after bubbling passes the root.
The React handler runs first, while the event bubbles through the root.

explanation: Since React 17, React attaches its listeners to the root container instead of `document`. When the native event bubbles to the root, React runs `onClick`, and `e.stopPropagation()` stops the native event too, so it never reaches the `document` listener. In React 16 the document listener would still have fired.
reference: react.dev: React 17 release notes (changes to event delegation)

options.why: `count` includes empty nodes such as null and false, but `toArray` drops them.
`Children.count` counts null and booleans as nodes, unlike `toArray`.
`toArray` removes empty nodes from its result.
Reversed: it is `count` that includes the empty nodes.

explanation: `Children.count` counts every node, including empty ones (null, undefined, booleans), so the answer is 3. `Children.toArray` returns only the nodes that would render, so its length is 1. Code that uses `count` to decide whether there are children can be fooled by `{cond && <X />}`.
